title: What Is Wrong with Your Eye
intro: Al-Khansa' mourns her brother Mu'awiya ibn Amr, killed by the two sons of Harmala of the tribe of Murra when he raided them; Tha'lab's recension of her diwan heads the poem as an elegy for Mu'awiya, and the poem itself says “if Murra has destroyed him”. Abu Ubayda held that she composed it for her brother Sakhr after his burial near Mount Asib, and al-Aghani quotes five of its lines as an elegy for Sakhr, then reports al-Sulami's objection: “This is not about Sakhr; she lamented her brother Mu'awiya with it, and Murra killed him.” It opens with eyes whose tears soak her robe and an oath to grieve for no one after him, then praises his courage and eloquence, his troops and horses, the poems he left, and the disasters he shouldered for his people, and ends with the women he set wailing like wild cows. Al-Aghani records that Ibn Surayj set some of its lines to music. Tha'lab's text has 38 lines; Osama Al-Waaedh recites the 31 lines of the Beirut printing, in its order.

translation: What is wrong with your eye, or with her?
The tears have soaked her robe.
1.sharh: She speaks to herself, asking what ails her eye, then speaks of herself as “her”, as if of another woman whose tears have wet her clothes. The Beirut printing's note takes the robe as the eye's own garment, its lid.

translation: After Ibn Amr, of the house of al-Sharid,
the earth has decked its burdens with him.
2.sharh: A question in form, a statement in meaning: now that Ibn Amr is buried, the earth has adorned its dead, its “burdens”, with him. Al-Asma'i read it the other way: the earth was rid of the weight of his galloping horsemen.

translation: I have sworn to grieve for no one who dies
and to ask no weeping woman what ails her.
3.sharh: Her loss has taken all her grief, so she will mourn no one else and ask no other mourner her sorrow; Tha'lab says everyone has the right to mourn after him. The Arabic leaves the “not” unsaid after the oath.

translation: By your father's life, what a young man he was:
with him war kindled its logs.
4.sharh: She swears to his worth: he was the fuel that set war ablaze and the man who ran it. Al-Mubarrad says she makes him the image of fierce burning, and its master.

translation: Sharp of spearhead, sharp of tongue,
he kept pace with every requital, paying back its like.
5.sharh: He was a fighter and a speaker both, and whatever was done to him, good or ill, he answered in kind. The word for requitals comes from qard, a loan, anything given that expects a return.

translation: I set my heart on every grave resolve;
woe to my soul, woe to it.
6.sharh: In her grief she resolved on the most desperate deeds: Tha'lab says to go raiding herself, a spur to her kin; al-Athram says to kill herself. “Woe to it” is a threat; al-Mubarrad says it is also what one says after a narrow escape.

translation: I will drive myself to a perilous course:
either it goes against me or for me.
7.sharh: She will throw herself into war for his sake, whatever the outcome, death or victory. Al-Asma'i, as Tha'lab reports, heard a reproach to her clan in it: if you will not act, I will stand in your place.

translation: If the soul is patient, it will find joy;
if the soul despairs, it is the more wretched.
8.sharh: Patience will in time bring back happiness, while despair only deepens her misery, so she turns back to endurance after the wild resolves of the lines before. The line is not in Tha'lab's text.

translation: We hold our lives cheap, and lives held cheap
on the day of battle last the longer.
9.sharh: Her people care nothing whether they live or die in battle, and that is what keeps them alive: Tha'lab records two readings, that it keeps their names alive, or that charging is safer than running away.

translation: We know that the deaths of men
will reach them wherever it pleases them.
10.sharh: Death will find every man in the end, so there is no sense in flight. The words “wherever it pleases them” are uncertain: the commentators do not explain them, and Tha'lab's text has “when a man is put to the test”.

translation: Let death now run its courses, after the young man
left lying at al-Mahw.
11.sharh: With him dead she no longer cares what fate does: let death go whichever way it likes, says Abu Ubayda. Al-Mahw is the place where he fell, and al-Bakri places it in the land of Murra.

translation: Many a heaving troop, its fair riders on top,
double mail upon it, ring matched with ring,
12.sharh: She turns to his battles: a troop so large it seems to sway, its horsemen covered in double-woven mail. The commentators do not explain the last word, “its likes”; the likelier sense is mail whose rings are doubled.

translation: like a dense rain-cloud banked with white,
throwing out cloud ahead and fed with cloud behind,
13.sharh: The troop is as massive as a storm cloud that sends cloud before it while more cloud joins it from behind; Tha'lab says she means that it has reinforcements.

translation: and many horses pressing on, heavy with mailed men,
whose champions you fought with the sword.
14.sharh: Horses weighed down with armoured riders, crowding forward one on another's heels, and he met their best men in single combat. Here she turns to address her brother directly.

translation: Many a poem as keen as a spear's edge
lives on, while the man who made it passes,
15.sharh: Her brother was a poet too: his verses cut like a spearhead and outlive their maker, as Tha'lab puts it, a poem outlasting its generation.

translation: splitting the crest of Yadhbul,
a peak that would never part from its ibexes.
16.sharh: His poem could split the summit of Mount Yadhbul, a peak so high and safe that its wild goats never leave it; Tha'lab calls this deliberate exaggeration.

translation: You spoke it, son of Amr, and made it smooth;
people have never spoken its like.
17.sharh: She speaks to him: the poem was his, easy on the tongue and unmatched. Tha'lab notes, on a line of this poem not recited here, that she makes him a poet as well as a generous horseman.

translation: If Murra has destroyed him,
he had killed many of them before.
18.sharh: His killers, the tribe of Murra, had paid dearly first: he had killed many of them. Murra killed Mu'awiya, as al-Sulami points out in assigning the poem to him rather than to Sakhr.

translation: The lofty mountains fell at his killing,
and the earth was shaken with its quaking.
19.sharh: His death was a catastrophe on the scale of the world: mountains collapsed and the earth shook. The second half echoes the words of the opening verse of the Quran's chapter of the Earthquake (99:1).

translation: The stars moved from their places at his loss,
and the sun was wrapped in its coverings.
20.sharh: The heavens mourned too: the stars were thrown out of place and the sun was eclipsed, as if covered by the cloth thrown over a horse.

translation: Many a calamity a wrongdoer brought on,
at which the pregnant women dropped their burdens,
21.sharh: She tells of disasters caused by others, so terrible that pregnant women miscarried in fear; Tha'lab stresses that the man who brought them on had no tie to her brother.

translation: Ibn Amr bore it, asking no one's help,
though others were nearer to it than you.
22.sharh: Her brother took the trouble on himself alone, though others were closer to it in kinship or in place, says Tha'lab; in the second half she addresses him again.

translation: It was not his before all others to bear,
but he shielded the clan from what struck it
23.sharh: It was not his duty above anyone else's, but as their chief he protected near and distant kin alike from what overwhelmed them; Tha'lab reads the future tense here as a past.

translation: in a battlefield narrow between the lines,
where Death trails her skirts.
24.sharh: He fought it out where the two forces met, in the thick of the killing. Tha'lab pictures Death strutting there, delighting in the fighting, where no one who falls between the lines comes out alive.

translation: You thrust at their horses, and when they turned,
you wet their haunches with blood.
25.sharh: He met the enemy horsemen face to face, and when they fled he speared them from behind, so that neither coming nor going did they escape; Tha'lab adds that the riders lay dead.

translation: Many white-skinned women you shielded on the morning of the cry,
lifting their skirts in terror,
26.sharh: On the morning of a raid, when the alarm went up, he protected the women, who gathered up their skirts to run, as Tha'lab and al-Kirmani explain.

translation: many hard-driven camels you drove from your saddle,
and branded the unmarked ones with your sword,
27.sharh: He drove herds of camels from the saddle, and his sword-cuts were the brand on the unbranded. In Tha'lab's text it is a troop he led, and his spear marked the haunches of its horses.

translation: many a swift she-camel, hard as the rock in a trough,
whose limbs you left on the sandy track,
28.sharh: He rode his camels so hard on his journeys that even the toughest of them gave out, and he left her where she fell on the sandy track; al-Mubarrad says the hardness of the journey left her there.

translation: on the way to a king, not to common men;
and that was her lot.
29.sharh: His journeys were to kings, never to lesser men, and wearing out his camel on such journeys was her portion. Tha'lab's text reads “that was what she was driven for”.

translation: You give your horses the enemies' land,
and on the raids they cast their foals.
30.sharh: He carried his raids into enemy country, says Tha'lab, and his mares, out on campaign, dropped their foals on the way.

translation: Many a band of wailing women you sent out like wild cows,
cows that have caught sight of their young.
31.sharh: He killed their men and sent the women out to mourn, wailing like wild cows lowing to their calves, says Mubtakir al-Tha'labi; Ya'qub ibn al-Sikkit says the likeness is in their wide eyes.

1.2.4.head: سِربال
1.2.4.meaning: Sirbal: a shirt or robe; the Beirut printing's note takes it as the eye's garment, its lid.

2.1.5-6.meaning: The house of al-Sharid, the poet's family within the tribe of Sulaym: she was the daughter of Amr ibn al-Harith ibn al-Sharid.

2.2.1.head: حَلّى
2.2.1.meaning: Adorned, from hilya, ornament; others read it as “unloaded”.

2.2.4.head: أَثقال
2.2.4.meaning: Athqal, “burdens”: the dead, as the Quran's “the earth brings out its burdens” (99:2) was understood.

3.1.1.head: آلى
3.1.1.meaning: I swore. Tha'lab's text has “for ever I will grieve”.

4.1.1-2.meaning: “By your father's life”: an oath. Tha'lab has “by his father's life”.

4.2.4.head: أَجذال
4.2.4.meaning: Ajdhal: stumps and roots of trees, burned as heavy firewood.

5.2.1.head: جارى
5.2.1.meaning: Keeps pace with. Tha'lab's text and the Beirut printing have yujazi, “repays”.

5.2.2.head: المَقارِض
5.2.2.meaning: Maqarid: what people pay one another back, good or ill, from qard, a loan.

6.2.3-4.meaning: Awla laha: a threat, “woe to her”; also said by someone who has just escaped a disaster.

7.1.4.head: آلَة
7.1.4.meaning: Ala: a state, a course. Al-Aghani has khutta, a plan.

9.1.3.head: هَون
9.1.3.meaning: Hawn: lightness, holding something cheap. Tha'lab has hun, contempt.

10.2.3.head: حَلِيَ
10.2.3.meaning: So the reciter and the Beirut printing; no commentator explains it. Tha'lab's text has hina yubla laha, “when a man is put to the test for them”.

11.2.2.head: المَحو
11.2.2.meaning: Al-Mahw: a wide, level plain; al-Bakri places it in the land of Murra and says Mu'awiya ibn Amr was killed there.

12.1.1.head: رَجراجَة
12.1.1.meaning: Rajraja: a troop so large it heaves and sways.

12.1.3.head: بيض
12.1.3.meaning: Bid, “the white”: its horsemen. Tha'lab reads bayd, helmets.

12.2.2.head: المُضاعَف
12.2.2.meaning: Double mail, woven two rings by two.

13.1.1.head: كِرفِئَة
13.1.1.meaning: Kirfi'a: heavy cloud piled layer on layer.

14.1.2.head: تَكَدَّسَ
14.1.2.meaning: Takaddas: press on heavily, one on another's heels, like ibexes climbing a mountain.

16.1.4.head: يَذبُل
16.1.4.meaning: Yadhbul: a mountain at the far edge of the land of the Kilab.

17.1.2-3.meaning: Son of Amr: her brother, Mu'awiya ibn Amr in Tha'lab's recension, Sakhr ibn Amr according to Abu Ubayda.

18.1.3.head: مُرَّة
18.1.3.meaning: Murra: a tribe of Dhubyan. Its men Hashim and Durayd, the sons of Harmala, killed Mu'awiya ibn Amr when he raided them.

20.2.3.head: أَجلال
20.2.3.meaning: Ajlal: the cloths thrown over horses; the sun is covered as if with one, eclipsed.

24.2.3.head: أَذيال
24.2.3.meaning: Her skirts: the spearheads and the sword-points, says Tha'lab.

26.1.4.head: الصِّياح
26.1.4.meaning: The cry of the raid. Tha'lab has al-sabah, “the morning”, the day of a dawn raid.

27.1.1.head: مُعمَلَة
27.1.1.meaning: Mu'mala: camels ridden hard. Tha'lab's text has mujmi'a, a troop.

28.1.2-3.meaning: “Like the she-ass of the pool”: the rock standing in a watering trough, a picture of hardness.

28.2.2.head: الخَلّ
28.2.2.meaning: Khall: a track through the sand.

29.1.5.head: سوقَة
29.1.5.meaning: Suqa: commoners, anyone below a king.

29.2.4.head: أُكل
29.2.4.meaning: Ukul: lot, portion; so the reciter and the Beirut printing. Tha'lab has i'malaha, “what she was driven for”; al-Mubarrad has iklalaha.

31.1.1.head: نَوح
31.1.1.meaning: Nawh: women who wail for the dead.

31.2.2.head: العين
31.2.2.meaning: Al-In: wild cows, named for their wide eyes.

31.2.3.head: أَشبال
31.2.3.meaning: Their young (ashbal, properly lion cubs). Some copies read asbalaha, the first rains.
